title: Case study: ride-hailing
objective: Find nearby drivers fast: bucket drivers into map cells and search only the rider's cell and its neighbours, instead of measuring every driver.

sources.title: H3 docs (Uber's open-source geospatial index, h3geo.org): Introduction
H3 docs: Aggregation (squares have neighbours at two different distances; hexagons' neighbours are all equidistant)

simplifies: This square-grid search is a plausible design, not Uber's actual architecture. What Uber has published is H3, its open-source index, which uses hexagonal cells; its docs explain that a square's 8 neighbours sit at two different distances, while all 6 of a hexagon's neighbours are equidistant. Real matching also weighs road distance, driver direction, ratings and surge pricing.

critique.prompt: A proposal: every driver's location ping is written to the main SQL database; matching runs "sort all drivers in the city by distance, take the first" for each ride request.

risks.text: Every location ping (every few seconds from every driver) hits the main database
risks.why: That write rate can overload the database every other part of the app depends on; live locations belong in a fast in-memory store.

risks.text: Sorting the whole city's drivers for every request gets slower as the city grows
risks.why: Search nearby cells instead: the work depends on how many drivers are close, not how many exist.

risks.text: Drivers send their location every few seconds
risks.why: Fresh locations are needed for good matches; the problem is where they're written, not that they're sent.

risks.text: Riders can see the driver's car moving on a map
risks.why: That's a feature built from the same live locations, not a risk.

critique.hint: Count the work: how many writes arrive, and how many drivers each match looks at.

options.text: Move live locations out of the main database into an in-memory store
options.explanation: Right. If the main database slows, everything slows: payments, trips, sign-ins.

options.text: Replace the city-wide sort with a nearby-cells search
options.explanation: Important, but slow matching hurts matching; an overloaded main database hurts everything.
Matches get worse, and the design problem is still there.

critique.explain: Fix the shared bottleneck first: high-rate location writes don't belong in the main database. Then make matching local: search a few nearby cells, which is what grid indexes like H3 make easy.

quiz.prompt: Why search grid cells instead of every driver?

options.text: Only drivers in a few nearby cells are measured, so the work stays small however big the city is
options.explanation: Right. A million drivers, and each search still looks at a handful.

options.text: Grid cells give more accurate distances
options.explanation: Each candidate's distance is still measured exactly; the grid just picks the candidates.
The grid is extra memory; the gain is speed.

quiz.prompt: Why does the search include the 8 neighbouring cells, not just the rider's own?

options.text: A driver just across a cell edge can be closer than one in the same cell
options.explanation: Right. With a radius up to one cell, every driver in range is in the rider's cell or a neighbour.

options.text: To find more drivers than needed
options.explanation: It finds exactly those in range; neighbours are only candidates.

options.text: Cells are too small to hold drivers
options.explanation: Cells hold drivers fine; edges are the issue.
